title: Knowing what good looks like
keyIdea: Before you start, find out what a good one needs. A good example shows you. A short list, called success criteria, says it in words. Use the list at the start to know your aim, and at the end to tick off your own work. Pretty is not the same as good.

kid: Before you make a thing, ask: what does a good one need? Then you know what you are aiming for.
Look at a good one first. A good card for Gran says To Gran. It has kind words and a picture. It says who it is from. Sparkles are nice, but a card can be good with none.
Make a list of what a good one needs. This list has a big name. It is called success criteria.
When you think you are done, check. Look at each line on the list. Is it there? Tick it. Is it not there? Add it. Then you are done.
adult: Teachers often share a learning intention (what we are learning, sometimes called WALT) and success criteria (what a good one needs, sometimes WILF). Many show a model piece too, called a WAGOLL: what a good one looks like. Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam name sharing the criteria for success as a core part of formative assessment. In England, Year 2 pupils are asked to evaluate their writing with the teacher and other pupils, and to re-read it to check it makes sense.

Young children often judge their work by how it looks or how it feels: it is neat, long, colourful, or they worked hard. Success criteria swap that feeling for a short list they can check. A good example makes the list concrete, because the child can point to each feature in it.

Common mistakes: thinking pretty, long or neat means good; saying done without checking; looking at the list only at the end, when it is too late to plan; and copying the model word for word instead of using it to see the features. Keep the list short, about three or four points, and in your child's own words.

In the lab your child taps the parts that make a good birthday card better than a sparkly one, builds the list and leaves out pretty extras, checks Ben's card line by line to find the missing part, fixes three cards from the crosses on the list, and makes a card while the list ticks itself.

familyTip: Before your child draws, builds or writes something, ask: what does a good one need? Agree two to four things and write them as a list with boxes. Look at a good one together if you have one. At the end, let your child tick the list, not you. If a box is empty, ask what they could add.

visual.caption: A good sentence: is each thing on the success list, or not needed? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: spot what makes a good card good, build the success list, tick off Ben's card, fix three cards and make your own.

choices: A list of what a good piece of work needs
A prize for the best work
The colours you have to use
practice.hint: Think of the list we made for a good birthday card.
practice.explain: Success criteria are a short list of what a good one needs, like who it is to, kind words, a picture and who it is from.

practice.prompt: The list for a good card has {a} things. Your card ticks {b} of them. How many more things do you need to add?
practice.hint: Count on from {b} up to {a}, or take {b} away from {a}.
practice.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}, so you need to add {=a-b} more things before every box has a tick.

practice.prompt: Ben says, "My card looks nice, so it is done." What should he do?
practice.hint: Looking nice is a feeling. What tells you for sure?
practice.explain: Ben should check each line on the list. His card had no kind words, and the list is how he finds that out.

practice.prompt: Kim writes {n} sentences. She checks each one for a full stop. {m} have no full stop. How many sentences do have a full stop?
practice.hint: Take the sentences with no full stop away from all {n}.
practice.explain: {n} − {m} = {=n-m}, so {=n-m} sentences have a full stop. Kim adds full stops to the other {m}.

choices: What A Good One Looks Like
Write And Go On Learning Lots
When All Groups Open Little Letters
pool.hint: It is a good example you look at before you start.
pool.explain: WAGOLL means What A Good One Looks Like: a good example that shows you what you are aiming for.

pool.prompt: When should you look at the success criteria?
choices: Before you start, and again at the end
pool.hint: One look tells you the aim. One look checks you got there.
pool.explain: Look first so you know what a good one needs. Look again at the end to tick off your own work.

pool.prompt: The list for a good story start has {a} things. Ola's story has {b} of them. How many are missing?
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b}, so {=a-b} things are missing. The list shows Ola which ones to add.

pool.prompt: Jay checks his work with a list of {a} things. He ticks {b} of them and puts a cross by the rest. How many crosses are there?
pool.hint: Every line gets a tick or a cross. Take the ticks away from all {a}.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} crosses. Each cross is a thing Jay still needs to add.

pool.prompt: Which one is on a success list for a good birthday card?
pool.hint: Which one does Gran need to know who sent it?
pool.explain: Who it is from is on the list. Glitter and size can be nice, but a card can be good without them.

pool.prompt: Mo looks at a good poster before he makes his own. Why?
choices: To see what a good one has, then make his own
pool.hint: A good example shows the parts to aim for.
pool.explain: Mo uses the good poster to spot what it has, like a big title and a picture. Then he makes his own poster with his own words.

pool.prompt: The list says: a capital letter, finger spaces, a full stop. Zak writes "I like dogs" with no dot at the end. What is missing?
pool.hint: Check each line of the list. Look at the very end of the sentence.
pool.explain: It starts with a capital I and has spaces, but there is no full stop at the end, so that box gets a cross.

pool.prompt: The list for a cat drawing says: ears, whiskers, a tail. Which drawing is better?
choices: The one with ears, whiskers and a tail
The one with sparkles but no tail
pool.hint: Tick off the list for each drawing.
pool.explain: The drawing with ears, whiskers and a tail ticks every box. Sparkles are not on the list.
